lesson.title: Forces come in pairs

steps.headline: A push always has a push back

lead.text: Go back to the skaters. When the first skater pushes, she exerts a force on the second skater. At the same moment the second skater exerts a force on her, of the same size and in the opposite direction. If she pushes with 25 N, he pushes back on her with 25 N. The second force is easy to miss because he does not seem to be doing anything, but it is what sends her backwards.

This is Newton's third law of motion. When object A exerts a force on object B, B exerts a force on A that is equal in size and opposite in direction. The two forces form a pair, and every force has a partner of this kind. You feel the partner whenever you push on something: a heavy door pushes back against your hand.
A and B are two skaters on smooth ice.

reveal.text: A push and its push back are the same size, so B pushes on A with 40 N.

steps.headline: The two forces act on different objects

lead.text: The forces in a pair are equal and opposite, so you might expect them to cancel. They do not, because they act on different objects. A's push acts on B and B's push acts on A. Forces cancel only when they act on the same object and we add them to find that object's net force. A force on A and a force on B never go into the same sum.
Signs record the opposite directions. Take right as positive. If A pushes B with +30 N, B pushes A with −30 N. The sizes match and the signs differ.

It is easy to mistake two forces on the same object for a pair. A book rests on a table. The weight pulls down on the book and the support force pushes up on the book. They can be equal and opposite, but both act on the book, so they are not a pair. The partner of the table's push up on the book is the book's push down on the table, and the partner of the book's weight is the book's own pull on the Earth.
Carts A and B sit on a track with A on the left.

Now ask what each skater does. The two forces are equal, but each acts on its own skater, so we apply the second law to each skater separately. A skater of mass m pushed with a force F accelerates at F ÷ m. Suppose two skaters push each other with 90 N and their masses are 30 kg and 45 kg. Their accelerations are 90 ÷ 30 = 3 m/s² and 90 ÷ 45 = 2 m/s².

The directions are opposite because the forces are. With right as positive, the 30 kg skater is pushed to the left and accelerates at −3 m/s². The 45 kg skater is pushed to the right and accelerates at +2 m/s².

afterFigure.text: The lighter skater gains velocity faster and moves off faster. A pair of equal forces does not give equal motion, because the second law divides each force by the mass of the object it acts on.

Divide the force on B by B's mass.

lead.text: Now look at the other cart. Cart A has mass 2 kg, and its only horizontal force is B's leftward push of 10 N. Right is positive.

reveal.text: The same size of force gave a bigger acceleration, because A has less mass.

steps.headline: Treating both objects as one system

lead.text: Sometimes it helps to draw a boundary round both objects and treat them as a single system. The pair of forces between the skaters is then inside the system. Add up the forces on the system and the pair cancels, because +F from one skater and −F from the other make zero. The pair cannot change the motion of the system as a whole, in the way that two people in a boat cannot move the boat by pushing on each other.

Each skater still accelerates, because each one has an unbalanced force acting on them. The cancelling happens only when both are counted together. To move the system as a whole, something outside it has to push, such as a third skater.

lead.text: Now treat the two carts as one system. Their pair of forces is inside it.

reveal.text: Inside one system the pair cancels, so it cannot change the system's overall motion. Each cart still accelerates because the pair acts on it alone.

lesson.orientation: Identify an interaction pair and explain why equal forces can produce different accelerations.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Two skaters stand face to face on smooth ice, both at rest. One of them puts her hands on the other's shoulders and pushes. The skater who was pushed glides backwards, which is what you would expect. The skater who did the pushing glides backwards too, in the opposite direction, although nobody pushed her.

A push on a wall does the same. Lean on a wall while standing on a skateboard and you roll away from it. The wall seems to do nothing, yet it must be pushing on you, because your velocity changed and the second law says that takes a net force.

This lesson looks at that second push, the one you do not see. We find out how big it is, which object it acts on and what it does to each skater. The last step treats the two skaters as one thing, to see what the pushes between them can and cannot do.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the partner of any force, and say why equal forces can still give different accelerations.

recap.keyIdea: Forces come in pairs, equal and opposite, on different objects. Equal forces give different accelerations when the masses differ.

blocks.text: You found that B pushes back on A with 40 N, and that a 3 kg cart and a 6 kg cart pushed apart by 12 N accelerate at 4 and 2 m/s² in opposite directions.

recap.nextHook: Surfaces push back along them as well as up. Next we see how friction decides whether a box slides.

questions.prompt: B pushes A left with a force of 10 N. Find the magnitude of A's force on B in newtons.
hints: Identify the two objects in the interaction.
The two forces have equal magnitudes.
The partner force has the same magnitude and opposite direction.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Newton's third law gives an equal magnitude: 10 N, directed right.

questions.onCorrect: 10 N. The partner force is equal in size and opposite in direction.

misconceptions.feedback: The forces do not cancel here: they act on different objects. Each is the same size.
The two forces have the same size. They are not added together.

questions.prompt: Cart A pushes a 5 kg cart B right with 10 N. This is B's only horizontal force. Find B's acceleration in m/s² with right positive.
hints: Apply the second law to B alone.
Divide the force on B by B's mass.
Divide the interaction force by B's mass.
questions.onCorrect: +2 m/s². Apply the second law to B alone: the force on B divided by B's mass.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies force by mass. Divide the force by B's mass.
B is pushed right, so its acceleration is positive.

questions.prompt: Cart A has mass 2 kg. Its only horizontal force is 10 N left. With right positive, find A's acceleration in m/s².
hints: Use the mass of the object being accelerated.
The leftward force has a negative sign.
Divide the leftward force magnitude by mass and retain its sign.
questions.onCorrect: −5 m/s². The force on A is leftward, so its acceleration is negative. Divide by A's mass.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but A is pushed left. With right positive, its acceleration is negative.
That multiplies force by mass. Divide the force by A's mass.

questions.prompt: Two carts, A and B, push each other and nothing else pushes on them horizontally. Why do their two forces cancel when we add up the forces on the pair of carts taken together?
hints: Choose a boundary containing both interacting objects.

acceptedIdeas: They are equal, opposite internal forces
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: For the combined system, the pair is internal and sums to zero. Each cart can still accelerate.

choices.label: They act on the same cart
They are equal, opposite internal forces

questions.onCorrect: They are equal, opposite internal forces. Inside the combined system they sum to zero, yet each cart still accelerates.

misconceptions.feedback: The two forces act on different carts, one on each. That is why each cart accelerates.
Each cart has an unbalanced force on it, so both accelerate. The cancelling is only for the pair taken together.

questions.prompt: Two carts interact with forces of magnitude 18 N. Cart B has mass 6 kg and no other horizontal force. Find its acceleration magnitude in m/s².
hints: Use the force acting on B.
Equal interaction forces do not require equal accelerations.
Divide the force magnitude by the mass of B.
questions.onCorrect: 3 m/s². B's acceleration is the force on B divided by B's mass.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies force by mass. Divide the force by B's mass.
The forces on the two carts do not cancel. Each acts on a different cart.

questions.prompt: A book rests on a table. Which force is the partner of the table's upward force on the book?
hints: A third-law pair acts on different objects.

acceptedIdeas: The book's downward force on the table
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The paired force swaps the two objects: book on table, opposite to table on book.

choices.label: Earth's downward gravitational force on the book
The book's downward force on the table

questions.onCorrect: The book's downward force on the table. A pair swaps the objects: table on book, book on table.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a different force on the same book. A pair always acts on two different objects, one force on each.
Mass is not a force. The partner of a force is another force.

questions.prompt: How hard does B push back on A, in newtons?
hints: Think of pushing a wall. Does the wall push back?
The push back is just as hard.
It has the same size as A's push.
questions.onCorrect: 40 N. Every push has a push back of the same size. That is Newton's third law.

questions.prompt: Why do the carts accelerate differently when the forces are equal?
hints: Read each choice against the situation before you answer.

acceptedIdeas: Acceleration is force divided by mass, and the masses differ.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Acceleration is force divided by mass, and the masses differ.

choices.label: Acceleration is force divided by mass, and the masses differ.
The heavier cart is pushed harder.
Equal forces only act on the lighter cart.

One force acts on each cart. They are equal in size.
